---
title: "Link functions"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

We have two scales to connect. On the response scale, the fitted probability of an *in* choice must remain between zero and one. On the regression scale, a sum such as $\beta_0+\beta_1x_i$ can take any real value. Recall that this sum is called the [**linear predictor**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214): it combines each predictor value with its coefficient and then adds the products.

We will write this sum as $\eta_i$. The symbol only gives the linear predictor a short name. We already use $x_i$ for an observed predictor and $y_i$ for an observed response, so using a third symbol keeps those three quantities distinct. The Greek letter adds no further mathematical assumption.

The basic idea is to use a reversible translation between the two scales. A [**link function**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) translates a conditional mean to the real line. Its **inverse link** translates the result back to the response scale. “Reversible” means that each allowable mean maps to exactly one regression-scale value and maps back to the same mean. This is what **one-to-one** means here.

The translation below uses odds before we develop them in detail. For current purposes, [odds](odds-and-log-odds.qmd) compare the probability of an *in* response with the probability of a *for* response, $p/(1-p)$. Log odds take the natural logarithm of that ratio. We will return to their interpretation before using them to interpret regression coefficients.

Before writing the formula, consider the two probabilities actually observed in the SuperTelicity verb groups. The code computes each probability from that group's *in* responses and then applies the proposed translations.

```{r}
#| label: observed-link-scales
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
observed_link_scales <- aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st, mean)
names(observed_link_scales)[[2L]] <- "probability_in"
observed_link_scales$odds_in <- with(
  observed_link_scales,
  probability_in / (1 - probability_in)
)
observed_link_scales$log_odds_in <- log(observed_link_scales$odds_in)
observed_link_scales
```

The group with probability below one half maps to negative log odds, while the group above one half maps to positive log odds. A probability of exactly one half would map to zero because its odds would be one.

The logit link performs exactly this translation. We continue with the SuperTelicity response, whose [measurement and row structure](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd) we have already worked through.

A potential worry is that the zero--one range uniquely forces this particular translation. It does not. The **link-choice problem** is that several reversible functions keep predictions in the correct range, while making different assumptions about how a change on the regression scale behaves near zero and one.

```{r}
#| label: load-and-fit-link
#| echo: true
st$duration_centered <- st$log_duration_minutes -
  mean(st$log_duration_minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
st <- st[!is.na(st$duration_centered), ]
fit <- glm(prep_in ~ duration_centered + verb_type,
           family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = st)
```

For a Bernoulli mean $0<\pi_i<1$, the logit link and its inverse are

$$
g(\pi_i)=\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=\eta_i,
\qquad
g^{-1}(\eta_i)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta_i}}=\pi_i.
$$

The inverse follows by exponentiating: $e^{\eta}=\pi/(1-\pi)$, so $e^\eta(1-\pi)=\pi$ and hence $\pi=e^\eta/(1+e^\eta)$. The logit is especially convenient because a coefficient is a log odds ratio. The probit instead uses $\Phi^{-1}(\pi)$, whereas the complementary log-log link $\log[-\log(1-\pi)]$ is asymmetric.

```{r}
#| label: compare-valid-bernoulli-links
#| echo: true
p <- sort(unique(aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st, mean)$prep_in))
data.frame(probability = p, logit = qlogis(p), probit = qnorm(p),
           complementary_log_log = log(-log(1 - p)))
```

The link acts on the conditional mean, not on the observed zeros and ones. The fitted SuperTelicity model supplies actual values on both scales.

```{r}
#| label: link-map
#| echo: true
observed <- aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st, mean)
observed$empirical_logit <- qlogis(observed$prep_in)
observed$round_trip_probability <- plogis(observed$empirical_logit)
observed
```

`qlogis()` maps the empirical group probabilities to real numbers, and `plogis()` returns them to the probability scale. These functions implement the equations above without transforming any response row.

## The inverse link keeps predictions valid

```{r}
#| label: plot-link-fit
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
grid <- expand.grid(
  duration_centered = seq(min(st$duration_centered), max(st$duration_centered),
                          length.out = 201L),
  verb_type = levels(st$verb_type)
)
grid$log_duration_minutes <- grid$duration_centered + mean(st$log_duration_minutes)
grid$eta <- predict(fit, newdata = grid, type = "link")
grid$probability <- plogis(grid$eta)
st$duration_bin <- cut(st$log_duration_minutes,
  unique(quantile(st$log_duration_minutes, probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 13L))),
  include.lowest = TRUE)
binned <- aggregate(cbind(prep_in, log_duration_minutes) ~ duration_bin + verb_type,
                    st, mean)
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = binned,
             aes(log_duration_minutes, prep_in, shape = verb_type), size = 1.7) +
  geom_line(data = grid,
            aes(log_duration_minutes, probability, linetype = verb_type),
            color = "#1F5A85", linewidth = .8) +
  labs(x = "Selected duration (log minutes)",
       y = "Probability of an in-completion", shape = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

The model is additive in $\eta_i$ but curved in $\pi_i$. A coefficient gives a constant change in log odds; the corresponding probability change varies with the baseline. The link leaves the Bernoulli support and observed response unchanged while connecting the linear predictor to the family mean.

For instance, the fitted result verb coefficient has different consequences for response probabilities at two duration values observed in the data. We use the first and third quartiles of the retained duration values and compare the fitted manner and result probabilities at each value.

```{r}
#| label: baseline-dependent-probability-change
#| echo: true
observed_duration_quartiles <- unname(quantile(
  st$duration_centered,
  probs = c(.25, .75)
))
contrast_rows <- data.frame(
  duration_centered = rep(observed_duration_quartiles, each = 2L),
  verb_type = factor(
    rep(c("manner", "result"), times = length(observed_duration_quartiles)),
    levels = levels(st$verb_type)
  )
)
contrast_rows$fitted_probability <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = contrast_rows,
  type = "response"
)
data.frame(
  duration_centered = observed_duration_quartiles,
  manner_probability = contrast_rows$fitted_probability[c(1L, 3L)],
  result_probability = contrast_rows$fitted_probability[c(2L, 4L)],
  result_minus_manner =
    contrast_rows$fitted_probability[c(2L, 4L)] -
    contrast_rows$fitted_probability[c(1L, 3L)]
)
```

For count means the analogous construction uses $\log\lambda_i=\eta_i$ and $\lambda_i=e^{\eta_i}>0$. Thus support constrains a link choice, but it does not determine that choice. The link maps a conditional mean between scales; the response family determines the modeled distributional shape.

## Recap and check

1. Does a Bernoulli response force the logit link? No. It forces predicted means into $(0,1)$; scientific and computational considerations distinguish valid links.
2. If a logit coefficient is one, is the probability change one? No. The coefficient is a one-unit log odds change, and the corresponding probability change depends on the baseline.

We can now assemble the response distribution, linear predictor, and link in the [generalized linear model](generalized-linear-models.qmd).
